India’s growth story is being built in steel, infrastructure, energy transition assets and industrial capacity. At the heart of that story is iron ore: a mineral that does not merely feed furnaces, but enables roads, railways, ports, cities, manufacturing and national resilience.

India’s growth story is being built in steel, infrastructure, energy transition assets and industrial capacity. At the heart of that story is iron ore: a mineral that does not merely feed furnaces, but enables roads, railways, ports, cities, manufacturing and national resilience.
In FY 2025-26, NMDC crossed a defining threshold, producing 53 million tonnes of iron ore and reinforcing its role as India’s largest iron ore producer. This achievement reflects more than scale. It reflects the strength of an integrated mining system: ore body knowledge, safe operations, processing capability, evacuation infrastructure, customer responsiveness and disciplined execution working together.
“Powering the Nation. Sustaining the Future.” captures this dual responsibility. NMDC is powering the nation by securing the raw material base for India’s steel-led development. It is sustaining the future by expanding with responsibility: investing in technology, improving operational efficiency, strengthening logistics, deepening environmental stewardship and preparing for a lower- impact, more resilient mining model.

As NMDC advances towards its long-term capacity ambition, the measure of progress will be broader than volume alone. It will be the Company’s ability to deliver reliable supply, disciplined growth, safer operations and responsible value creation. That is the promise of this year’s theme: building the materials of national progress while protecting the foundations of tomorrow.

Dear Stakeholders,
It gives me immense pleasure to present the Annual Report of NMDC Limited for FY 2025-26, a year marked by strong performance, significant milestones and continued progress towards our long-term vision.

It gives me immense pleasure to present the Annual Report of NMDC Limited for FY 2025-26, a year marked by strong performance, significant milestones and continued progress towards our long-term vision.
The year 2026 has marked an important chapter in our national journey. Despite global economic and geopolitical uncertainties, India’s progress remains steady and decisive. Our real GDP growth of 7.7% in FY26 reflects the strength of our economy and investment momentum. India is also asserting leadership in technology, innovation and global partnerships.

For NMDC, this has been a year replete with ‘Eureka’ moments where we discovered and rediscovered our true calling and embarked on a journey of profound transformation to harness our real potential. In FY26, we became the first mining company in India to produce more than 50 million tonnes of iron ore in a single year, achieving record production of 53.16 million tonnes and sales of 50.24 million tonnes, scripting history on stone. The numbers reflect an increase of 20.62% in production and 13.15% in sales year on year, which have been achieved organically, by optimizing and exceeding the capacities and capabilities of the existing production and sales equipments and infrastructure. NMDC has proved its resilience with such a quantum jump in production in a single year which is unprecedented and unparalleled in the industry. Through this commendable performance, NMDC has genuinely contributed to the strengthening of the foundation for India’s infrastructure and industrial growth.

This operational excellence was naturally reflected in the financial performance of the Company which registered new echelons in turnover and other financial parameters.. Revenue from operations increased by 33.31% to `31,554 crore, Profit After Tax rose by 10.88% to `7,421 crore and Net Worth increased by 14.39% to `33,836 crore. NMDC invested `3,384 crore in capital expenditure during the year while continuing to create value for shareholders through a proposed total dividend of `3.50 per share for FY 2025- 26, subject to shareholders’ approval.
India’s rapid industrialisation calls for secure, reliable and responsibly managed mineral resources. Our Vision 2030 of achieving 100 MTPA of iron ore production capacity is therefore not merely a business ambition, but an important contribution towards India’s long-term mineral security and economic growth.

Technology, Sustainability and People

Technology, Sustainability and People
State of Art Technology and innovation are an integral part of NMDC’s operations with an objective to improving operational visibility, decision-making, productivity and safety. Initiatives taken up include Digital Project Management Unit, Automated Sampling, Digitally Enabled Drilling and Blasting, Real-Time Material Visibility and Integrated Sustainability Data Systems.
Our commitment to responsible growth remains equally strong. NMDC is pursuing greater energy and resource efficiency, increased renewable energy utilisation, improved water and land stewardship and lower-carbon logistics. Our Net Zero Strategy and Roadmap provides a structured direction for reducing the environmental footprint of our operations.
Our people remain at the heart of this transformation. Safety continues to be a non- negotiable priority, complemented by focused investments in human capital through skill development, leadership enhancement and digital capabilities. Through our CSR initiatives, NMDC also continues to contribute to healthcare, education, skill development and community infrastructure, particularly in the regions surrounding our operations.

Corporate Governance
Corporate governance remains a cornerstone of NMDC’s organisational ethos, underpinning every aspect of our operations and decision-making. We are committed to creating sustainable long-term value for all our stakeholders including shareholders, customers, suppliers, creditors, the Government of India, State Governments, regulatory authorities, and the communities we serve. Guided by the highest standards of integrity and accountability, we strive to ensure full compliance with applicable laws and regulations, both in letter and spirit. Through transparent governance practices, prudent risk management and responsible decision-making, we continue to strengthen stakeholder confidence and safeguard value creation.
Looking Ahead
The year ahead will be the year of execution, consolidation and transformation. Stabilising our higher production base, reaching the 60 MT production milestone, completing critical infrastructure projects and advancing the next phases of capacity expansion will remain key priorities.

The journey towards 100 MTPA will require operational excellence, disciplined capital allocation, strong project execution, technology adoption and unwavering commitment to safety and sustainability. At the same time, NMDC will continue to explore opportunities for diversification into critical and strategic minerals, both domestically and internationally, in alignment with India’s evolving mineral security needs.
I am confident that NMDC has the resources, capabilities and institutional strength to meet the opportunities and challenges ahead. We are building an enterprise that is larger in scale, stronger in capability, smarter through technology and more responsible in its operations.

THE 100 MILLION TONNE MOMENTUM: SCALING FOR A VIKSIT BHARAT
The five-year performance trajectory of NMDC Limited for the period concluding 31st March 2026 provides empirical evidence of an enterprise in the midst of a historic transformation. This snapshot does not merely record financial and physical metrics; it narrates the story of how India’s premier Navratna mining

enterprise has successfully transitioned from around 34 million tonne (MT) in financial year 2020-21 to breaching the monumental 50 million tonne production threshold and finishing with 53+ MT in the current fiscal year. This momentum serves as the definitive operational foundation for our “Vision 2030,” which aims to double our current capacity to 100 million tonnes per annum to safeguard the resource security of a Viksit Bharat. By maintaining a disciplined focus on volume-led growth and cost-competitiveness— operating at one of the lowest cash costs globally—we have ensured that our financial performance remains resilient against the cyclical volatilities of the global iron ore market.

FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE: CAPITAL FORTITUDE AND EARNINGS RESILIENCE
NMDC’s financial performance over this five-year horizon reflects a philosophy of “financial fortitude,” where robust revenue generation funds aggressive capital expansion. From a turnover of approximately Indian Rupees 15,370 crore in financial year 2020-21, our revenue

NMDC’s financial performance over this five-year horizon reflects a philosophy of “financial fortitude,” where robust revenue generation funds aggressive capital expansion. From a turnover of approximately Indian Rupees 15,370 crore in financial year 2020-21, our revenue
from operations has more than doubled to Indian Rupees 31,554 crore in financial year 2025-26, a compound annual growth of roughly 15.5% and a 33.31% increase over the Indian Rupees 23,668 crore recorded in financial year 2024-25. Profit After Tax rose to Indian Rupees 7,421 crore in financial year 2025-26, a growth of 10.88%, with EBITDA strengthening to Indian Rupees 10,737 crore on the back of record production of 53.16 million tonnes and sales of 50.24 million tonnes. Net worth has expanded to Indian Rupees 33,836 crore and earnings per share to Indian Rupees 8.44, supporting a dividend of Indian Rupees 3.50 per share while sustaining an ambitious Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) roadmap towards 2030.

Profitability widened the choices
NMDC entered FY 2025-26 with a demanding financial equation. It had to support a step-up in iron ore production, continue a large mine-and-logistics build-out, fund the working requirements of a broader operating mix and maintain shareholder returns—all while remaining exposed to commodity prices, statutory levies and project timing. The year’s outcome materially improved the Company’s room to manoeuvre. Revenue from operations rose by 33.3% to `31,553.70 crore, profit after tax increased by 10.9% to `7,421.24 crore and operating cash flow more than tripled to `4,926.12 crore.

The value of this performance lies not only in the higher absolute numbers. It lies in what they allow NMDC to do next. Higher earnings increase the pool of internally generated capital available for expansion; stronger cash flow reduces the extent to which project delivery must rely on external funding; and a larger net-worth base gives the balance sheet more capacity to absorb market or execution shocks. Financial capital therefore sits behind each of NMDC’s other capitals: it pays for processing and evacuation assets, digital systems, skills, safety controls, community programmes and environmental management before those investments begin to produce their intended return.

Shareholders also participated in the year’s performance. NMDC paid dividends of `3,077.13 crore during FY 2025-26, compared with `2,901.30 crore in the previous year. Capital allocation follows operating readiness

Capital allocation follows operating readiness
NMDC’s Vision 2030 envisages iron ore production capacity of 100 MTPA. As at 31st March 2026, the Company had secured environmental-clearance capacity of 64.8 MTPA, supplemented by 17 MTPA through the NMDC-CMDC joint venture across Deposit-13 and Deposit-4. Closing the remaining capacity gap requires coordinated investment across mine augmentation, processing, evacuation, housing and digital capability. During the year, execution advanced on Screening Plant III at Kirandul, Screening Plant II at Donimalai, the slurry pipeline project, crushing and conveying facilities and railway infrastructure. Each project draws cash before it generates throughput, making sequencing as important as sanction.

The appropriate discipline is stage-gated rather than purely budget-led. A processing plant cannot create value if mine readiness, utilities or evacuation lag; a rail or slurry system cannot release its full benefit unless upstream ore and downstream handling are available; and a digital platform cannot improve decisions if data ownership and user adoption remain weak. Financial capital is protected when projects are tested against permissions, engineering maturity, contracting, interdependent packages, commissioning readiness and expected cash generation. This is why NMDC’s Digital Project Management Unit, which monitors projects and packages above `30 crore, is also a financial- control mechanism: earlier visibility over slippage can protect capital productivity.
Liquidity is a strategic reserve

Liquidity is a strategic reserve
Rapid expansion can make a profitable Company cash-constrained if working capital and construction outflows move ahead of collections and commissioning. NMDC’s financial-risk framework therefore matters alongside headline profitability. The audited statements describe credit assessment, ageing and expected-credit-loss review, rolling cash-flow forecasts, treasury limits and the management of surplus funds under applicable guidelines and Company policy. These controls are designed to preserve the ability to meet operating obligations, withstand volatility and continue priority projects without being forced into value-destructive financing or delayed maintenance.

The stronger FY 2025-26 net-worth position—`33,835.62 crore, up 14.4%—provides a larger cushion, but it does not remove commodity, execution or transition risk. The financial-capital story is therefore not one of surplus cash waiting to be spent; it is one of competing claims that must be prioritised against risk-adjusted value.
Road ahead: convert strength into returns
The next test is the quality of deployment. NMDC must keep funding the assets that remove real operating constraints, complete high-progress projects before fragmenting capital across too many new starts and protect maintenance and safety expenditure during the build-out. The Company must also continue to distinguish capacity, commissioned capacity, operating throughput and sales evacuation in its investment decisions. These are different stages of value creation, and financial returns emerge only when they align.

For investors, the most useful evidence will be a clearer bridge from annual capex to project milestones, commissioning, incremental throughput, cash conversion and return on capital employed. FY 2025-26 strengthened the financial platform: revenue, earnings, cash flow and net worth all increased. The enduring outcome will depend on whether that platform is converted into assets that start on time, operate reliably and generate sufficient cash to fund the next phase while continuing to reward shareholders.

The asset system moved more ore
Ore must pass through drilling, blasting, loading, crushing, screening, quality control, stockpiling and dispatch; the weakest stage can limit the value created by all the others.
FY 2025-26 demonstrated what manufactured capital is meant to do: convert geological resources and installed capability into a larger, deliverable volume of product. Iron ore production reached 53.16 MT, up 20.6%, while sales increased by 13.2% to 50.24 MT. The difference between the two growth rates is a reminder that production alone does not define the strength of a mining system.

This operating reality shapes NMDC’s Vision 2030 build-out. The ambition is not a single mine-capacity number but a coordinated network of brownfield augmentation, new deposits, processing facilities and evacuation infrastructure. By 31st March 2026, NMDC had environmental-clearance capacity of 64.8 MTPA, with a further 17 MTPA at the NMDC-CMDC joint venture’s Deposit-13 and Deposit-4. Turning that permissioned capacity into reliable production requires plants, conveyors, railway lines, slurry systems, utilities and people to be ready together. Manufactured capital is therefore managed as a chain, not as an inventory of projects.
Kirandul: adding capacity and flow
At the Kirandul Complex, Screening Plant III reached 82% overall progress by year-end. The Rapid Wagon Loading System package had been completed and was operating, while work continued on the main receiving substation, dry circuit, wet circuit and miscellaneous buildings. The loading system begins to strengthen dispatch capability, but the project’s full value depends on the remaining technological and supporting packages being completed, integrated and commissioned. Reporting a single progress percentage is useful; understanding which packages are already productive and which still govern the critical path is more useful.

The new crushing plant and downhill conveyor system for Deposits 14 and 11C was at an earlier stage, with 16% progress at 31st March 2026. These assets are intended to move ore from the deposit through crushing and controlled downhill conveying rather than relying only on conventional haulage. The near-term manufactured-capital effect is construction and work-in- progress; the expected operating effect is a more continuous material flow, with potential benefits for haulage efficiency, equipment deployment and safety. Those benefits should be evidenced after commissioning rather than assumed from the technology choice.

Process knowledge extends the resource

Process knowledge extends the resource
The R&D Centre at Hyderabad carries geological understanding into mineral processing and product development. The current-year MDA confirms its status as a Centre of Excellence recognised by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization and the Board’s Report confirms recognition by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research. Its work spans mineral processing, beneficiation, pelletisation, process flowsheets, mineralogy, material handling, metallurgical studies of iron ore and coal, chemical analysis and process improvement. Laboratory and pilot-scale facilities allow an operating problem to be studied before a full-scale intervention is made.
Remote sensing broadens the field of view. It can help interpret terrain, landform and change across areas that are difficult to observe continuously from the ground. Drone surveys add higher-resolution operational data, while geostatistics helps convert sampled information into spatial estimates. The tools do not eliminate geological uncertainty; they make it more explicit and manageable. Their value should be judged through decisions such as where to drill next, how to sequence a pit, how closely planned and actual grade reconcile, and where geotechnical or environmental attention is required.

This capability becomes more important as ore characteristics vary and lower-grade material must be considered. NMDC is developing facilities for dry beneficiation, which the MDA links to water-efficient processing of low-grade ores, and it is expanding capability to characterise and test critical minerals. The intellectual-capital effect is optionality: better characterisation and process routes may enable material that is currently difficult or uneconomic to be reassessed under different technical and market conditions. Realised value, however, depends on recovery, quality, energy, water, capital cost and scale—not on research activity alone.

Scale tests the quality of stewardship

Scale tests the quality of stewardship
Iron ore production rose by 20.6% to 53.16 MT in FY 2025-26. That achievement increased the amount of material moved and the demand placed on equipment, energy, water, land and environmental controls. Natural capital therefore cannot be described only through conservation programmes. It must be read alongside operating scale: whether resource use and emissions grow faster or slower than output, whether local impacts remain within permission and control, and whether rehabilitation progresses while the mine is active rather than being deferred to closure.
The year’s evidence is mixed in a useful way. Total energy consumption increased by 9.2% and Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 5.7%, but both grew more slowly than production and their physical intensities improved. Water consumption fell by 7.4% on the restated comparative basis and physical intensity declined from 0.21 to 0.16 KL per tonne, even as total water withdrawal increased. The story is therefore neither unqualified improvement nor deterioration: NMDC produced more with lower reported intensity, while its absolute energy and emissions footprint remained larger.

Committee Architecture
NMDC’s governance architecture is evolving with the enterprise it oversees. A larger mineral portfolio, coal operations, complex processing and logistics projects, international mineral scouting, digital integration and the 2040 transition horizon require oversight that extends beyond statutory compliance to the quality, resilience and accountability of strategic choices.
The Board’s role architecture provides lenses across finance, costing and taxation; mining, safety and environment; steel and metallurgy; people and law; digital transformation; social responsibility; strategy; production; commercial decisions; and public policy. Independent Directors add challenge on risk, audit, stakeholder interests and conduct.
Board committees create depth in specialised areas. The Audit Committee examines financial reporting, internal controls, audit findings, the Whistle Blower mechanism and related-party transactions. The Risk Management Committee oversees the enterprise risk framework and treatment of material exposures. The CSR & Sustainability Committee considers statutory CSR responsibilities and broader sustainability matters.

As a Central Public Sector Enterprise, NMDC operates within a distinctive appointment and accountability framework. Directors are appointed by the President of India through the Ministry of Steel and their terms are governed by applicable Government policies. The Board combines executive knowledge of the business, Government nominee perspective and independent oversight, giving the Company a governance structure suited to public-sector accountability and commercial execution.
As NMDC scales, collective Board capability is being applied to project and commissioning governance, digital and cyber resilience, climate transition, global mineral partnerships and the interdependence of operating, social and natural capital. A specialist director deepens discussion, while Board-wide understanding supports the scrutiny of assumptions and trade-offs in major capital, digital, risk and sustainability decisions.
The Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee focuses on investor and stakeholder service, while the Nomination & Remuneration Committee operates within the appointment and remuneration framework applicable to a Government company. The Board-approved ESG Committee operates at management level under the chairmanship of the Director (Production), coordinating ESG Policy implementation, monitoring initiatives and connecting functional action.

UMLMSS is a technology-driven platform designed for vehicle movement in mining operations through automated monitoring, digital validation and real- time analytics. Using drones, DGPS, advanced sensors and intelligent blast design software, the system enables accurate terrain mapping, optimized drill and charging patterns, real-time tracking of drilling and blast performance and post-blast analysis of fragmentation, vibration, throw and environmental parameters to support continuous operational improvement and optimum resource utilization.

2. Digital Twin of Mines:
The Digital Twin solution is a high-resolution digital representation of the mining environment designed to enhance operational efficiency, monitoring and data-driven decision-making. Leveraging drone-based surveys, geospatial technologies, cloud computing and advanced analytics, the system enables visualization and analysis of mine operations, including production monitoring, volumetric assessments, haul road and slope safety analytics, drainage analysis and environmental monitoring.
The above solution has been implemented at Bacheli, Kirandul, Donimalai and Panna Mines.

NMDC has set ambitious targets to achieve iron ore production of 60 million tonnes in FY 2027 with the ultimate goal of reaching 100 million tonnes by 2030. This endeavor will involve substantial capital investments to expand and enhance the company’s mining capabilities and infrastructure, along with a special focus of sustainability, society & environment. Additionally, the company plans to diversify into minerals other than iron ore, which are essential for the energy security and net-zero ambitions of the country.
NMDC Limited, established in November 1958, plays a pivotal role in the Indian mining and minerals sector. The company produces high-quality iron ore with a premium grade of 64% Fe and maintains a strong financial position, enabling significant investment capacity. More than 67 years of its experience, NMDC has successfully navigated challenging terrains and difficult market conditions and is continuously expanding its global reach. Strategically located near key demand centers, NMDC operates with one of the lowest cash costs (C1) in the industry, making it highly competitive against global counterparts in the iron ore business.

NMDC is dedicated to optimizing its operations and innovating processes to enhance efficiency throughout the organization. The Company recorded a Profit (before tax) of ` 10,155 crores in FY’26 and a net worth of ` 33,836 crores (as of 31.03.2026). NMDC has a rich history of rewarding investors with dividends. NMDC, India’s largest iron ore producer, continued its strong performance during FY 2025–26, becoming the first iron ore mining company in the country to surpass the 50 million tonne milestone. Global economy has been facing major headwinds due to ongoing conflict in the Middle East and associated supply chain disruptions. The Government’s continued emphasis on capital expenditure, logistics enhancement, digital infrastructure, renewable energy and industrial competitiveness is expected to strengthen the country’s long-term growth prospects. 2.2. Industry Overview
India’s steel industry continued its strong growth trajectory in FY26, supported by robust domestic demand from infrastructure, construction, manufacturing, automotive and capital goods sectors. Crude steel production increased to ~168 million tonnes during FY2614, registering a growth of around 10.7% over the previous year, while finished steel consumption rose by 7-8% to about 164 million tonnes15. The sustained growth in steel consumption reflects the continued momentum in economic activity and the Government’s focus on infrastructure development.
2.2.1 Global Steel Industry
Global crude steel production softened in 2025 at 1,849 million tonnes8, ~ 5.8% below the peak global output of 1,963 million tonnes in 20219. Key producers – including China, Japan, Russia and South Korea- recorded declines while India and the US recorded increase in crude steel production by 10.4% & 3% respectively.

In 2025, China’s steel exports increased by 14.1%, reaching 133.6 million tonnes from 117.1 million tonnes in 2024. Global apparent steel use has declined from 1,751 million tonnes in 2024 to 1,718 million tonnes in 202510. Building and infrastructure sector contributed 52% to the global steel use, followed by mechanical equipment at 16% and automotive at 12%11.
Driven by robust domestic demand, Indian steelmakers continued to expand their capacities during FY26, increasing the country’s total installed steelmaking capacity to ~220 MTPA. These investments, coupled with the ramp-up of existing facilities, further strengthened India’s position as the world’s second-largest crude steel producer. Despite this progress, per capita steel consumption in India reached 109 kg in 202516, well below the global average of 209 kg in 202517, underscoring considerable headroom for long-term demand growth. To unlock this potential, the country has set an ambitious target of raising per capita steel consumption to 160 kg by FY3118.
The World Steel Association forecasts that global demand is expected to grow by 0.3% in 2026 as well as 2.2% in 202712. It projects a turnaround in steel demand across developed economies, including the European Union, the US, Canada, Japan and Korea. • India’s per capita steel consumption at approximately 109 kg remains well below the world average of ~209 kg22, providing substantial headroom for growth. Increasing urbanization, expanding rural infrastructure, multiple key initiatives by the government along with a host of consumption enablers are expected to drive up the steel demand in key end-use sectors. Government initiatives for Self-Reliant India creating new avenues to set-up new industries is leading to demand in iron and steel.
The growth in steel production was accompanied by higher iron ore output, which crossed the 300 million tonne mark during FY26. As India’s largest iron ore producer, NMDC continued to play a pivotal role in supporting the country’s growing steel industry’s iron ore demand. The Company achieved a historic milestone by becoming the first mining company in India to surpass the 50 million tonne annual production mark, recording its highest-ever iron ore production of 53.15 million tonnes, a growth of 21% over the previous year.

• The Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Specialty Steel in India expands on the original 2021 framework (PLI 1.0) through subsequent phases like PLI 1.1 and PLI 1.2. It aims to boost domestic value-added steel manufacturing, reduce import dependence and offer financial incentives ranging from 4% to 15%. PLI 1.2 was launched on 04.11.2025, covering 22 product sub-categories under four product categories, namely: (i) Steel Grades for Strategic Sector, (ii) Commercial Grades – Category 1, (iii) Commercial Grades – Category 2 and (iv) Coated & Wire Products. The scheme offers incentive rates ranging from 4% to 15% for a period of five years, commencing from FY 2025–26, with incentive disbursement starting from FY 2026–27. The Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for specialty steel continues to attract investment, with committed capex from major steel producers, directly expanding the iron ore demand base.

On the trade front, FY26 marked a significant turnaround as India regained its status as a net exporter of finished steel. Finished steel exports increased to around 6.6 million tonnes with a surge of 35.9%, while imports declined sharply by 31.7%19. The improvement was supported by stronger export demand from key markets in West Asia, Europe and Southeast Asia, coupled with policy measures aimed at safeguarding domestic industry interests. During the year, the Government imposed a 12% safeguard duty on select steel products to address the surge in low-priced imports and support domestic producers20.
However, iron ore exports declined by ~13% to 26 million tonnes, while imports surged by more than 70% to 12 - 12.5 million tonnes21 as iron ore production growth lagged the steel output growth.
Looking ahead, the outlook for the Indian steel sector remains positive, driven by sustained investments in infrastructure, urbanisation, housing, transportation and renewable energy projects. NMDC’s Research & Development Centre, located at Hyderabad, continues to play a pivotal role in advancing mineral processing technologies, sustainable iron-making solutions and value addition from mining waste. Recognized as a “Centre of Excellence” by the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the R&D Centre reflects NMDC’s commitment towards technology- driven growth, sustainability and national mineral security.

Flagship R&D Projects 2025-26: 1. Development of New Products
The R&D Centre is equipped with state-of-the-art laboratories and pilot-scale facilities covering mineral beneficiation, automated mineral analysis, bulk solids flow studies, pelletization and agglomeration, analytical characterization, coal and coke- making studies and extractive metallurgy. Advanced analytical infrastructure includes X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Wavelength Dispersive X-ray Fluorescence (WD-XRF), Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-AES), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Automatic Mineral Analyser (AMA) and other specialized facilities.
Geopolymer Bricks from Mine Waste
The R&D Centre successfully developed high-strength geopolymer bricks utilizing iron ore tailings, overburden and mine waste. The cement-free bricks demonstrated excellent mechanical properties while significantly reducing carbon footprint, supporting sustainable waste-to-resource conversion.
Fused Magnesia from Kimberlite Tailings
The Centre’s NABL-accredited Chemical Laboratory (ISO 17025:2017) and DSIR recognition continue to strengthen its research capabilities and industry credibility. Modernization initiatives undertaken at the Patancheru facility during the year further enhanced the Centre’s analytical and pilot-scale research capacity.

In collaboration with CSIR–IMMT, Bhubaneswar, a laboratory- scale process was developed for extraction of fused magnesia from kimberlite tailings generated from diamond mining operations. The project supports import substitution and domestic production of magnesium-based refractory materials.
The R&D Centre extends technical support to NMDC’s mining and pelletization operations while also serving domestic and international public and private sector organizations. Collaborative research with premier institutions such as CSIR-IMMT and the University of Hyderabad supports innovation in beneficiation, waste utilization, circular economy initiatives and sustainable mineral processing technologies.

h. Share Transfer System

h. Share Transfer System
With effect from 01.04.2019, requests for transfer of securities shall be processed only in those cases where the securities are held in dematerialized form with a depository, in terms of guidelines issued by SEBI. Further, in terms of SEBI circular dated 25.01.2022, while processing investor service requests such as transmission, transposition, renewal, exchange, sub-division, consolidation and issue of duplicate certificates etc., the securities shall be issued in dematerialized form only. Accordingly, all shareholders of the Company are requested to convert their shareholdings from physical form to demat form at the earliest to reap the benefits of dematerialization. Requests for dematerialization of shares are processed and confirmation is given to the respective depositories viz, NSDL and CDSL within 15 days.

SEBI vide Circular dated 03.11.2021, has inter-alia made it mandatory for holders of physical securities to furnish/update PAN, email address, mobile number, bank account and nomination details, besides linking their PAN with Aadhar. The said circular also prescribes that those folios wherein any one or more of the aforesaid details are not available on or after 30.09.2023 shall be frozen and the investor will not be eligible to lodge grievance or avail service request from R&TA and will not be eligible for receipt of dividend. In view of the same, members holding shares in physical mode are requested to furnish PAN, KYC details and nomination forms immediately to the Company / R&TA in the prescribed forms available on the website of the Company www.nmdc.co.in. 3.2% 3.06% NMDC has invested in the development of a microwave-assisted hydrogen-based iron ore reduction technology aimed at enabling a low- carbon ironmaking process. Technology seeks to replace conventional carbon-based reductants with hydrogen, thereby reducing carbon dioxide emissions associated with iron ore reduction. In addition, microwave- assisted heating is expected to improve energy efficiency through rapid and uniform heat transfer, resulting in optimized process performance and lower energy consumption.

Capex 32.59% 28.80% As part of its sustainability-driven CAPEX strategy, NMDC continues to invest in advanced technologies aimed at improving environmental and social outcomes across its mining operations. A key initiative in this direction is the development of slurry pipeline infrastructure for transportation of iron ore fines.

To complement the existing Kirandul–Kothavalasa (K-K) railway system, NMDC has adopted slurry pipeline transport from its Bailadila mines. This system converts iron ore fines into a concentrated slurry, which is transported through pipelines to downstream processing facilities. At terminal locations, the slurry is filtered to produce pellet feed concentrate, subsequently used in pellet manufacturing for the iron and steel sector.
This CAPEX initiative aligns with global best practices and delivers significant sustainability benefits. It minimizes land disturbance through underground pipeline infrastructure, reduces dependency on traditional logistics and supports lower Scope 3 emissions. The process also enables efficient utilization of low-grade fines and slimes, thereby reducing mineral wastage and promoting circular resource use. Additionally, the pipeline ensures reliable, weather-independent transportation, improving operational resilience and enabling accessibility from remote mining locations.

b. What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine basis by the entity?
NMDC has established structured processes to identify work‑related hazards and assess risks for both routine and non‑routine activities across its mining operations.

NMDC has established structured processes to identify work‑related hazards and assess risks for both routine and non‑routine activities across its mining operations.
For routine activities such as drilling, blasting, excavation and material handling, hazard identification and risk assessment are carried out through site‑specific Safety Management Plans, Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and Job Safety Analysis (JSA). These processes take into account operational and environmental conditions, enabling the identification of hazards and implementation of appropriate control measures.
For non‑routine and high‑risk activities, including maintenance, shutdowns and emergency interventions, additional controls are applied through permit‑to‑work systems, task‑specific risk assessments and supervisory approvals, ensuring risks are assessed prior to execution and managed effectively.

For non‑routine and high‑risk activities, including maintenance, shutdowns and emergency interventions, additional controls are applied through permit‑to‑work systems, task‑specific risk assessments and supervisory approvals, ensuring risks are assessed prior to execution and managed effectively.
Risk identification and mitigation measures are further supported by periodic review mechanisms. Project audit teams conduct internal safety audits twice a year, ensuring a secure work environment by reviewing compliance and following up on audit findings. Additionally, all projects undergo quarterly equipment inspections and monitoring, overseen by dedicated teams to ensure operational stability and safety. These processes are part of NMDC’s integrated safety management framework, supporting systematic identification, assessment and mitigation of occupational health and safety risks.
c. Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from such risks. (Y/N)
Yes.
NMDC has established processes for workers to report work-related hazards and unsafe conditions through supervisors, shift in-charge and site-level reporting mechanisms, where such concerns are formally recorded and addressed.

NMDC has established processes for workers to report work-related hazards and unsafe conditions through supervisors, shift in-charge and site-level reporting mechanisms, where such concerns are formally recorded and addressed.
The Company’s occupational health and safety framework, aligned with ISO 45001:2018, incorporates Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) methodologies and standard safety mechanisms commonly adopted in the mining sector. These include permit-to-work (PTW) systems for high-risk and non-routine activities, job safety analysis (JSA), toolbox talks, workplace inspections and Lock-out Tag-out (LOTO) procedures to ensure safe isolation of energy sources during maintenance and repair activities.
Workers are encouraged to proactively report unsafe conditions and are empowered to stop work and remove themselves from situations posing serious risk to their health and safety until appropriate controls are implemented, without fear of retaliation.
These processes are supported by periodic safety audits, equipment inspections, safety meetings and supervisory oversight, ensuring continuous monitoring and mitigation of occupational health and safety risks.

NMDC Limited adopts structured waste management practices in line with applicable environmental regulations and Government of India guidelines.
Mining waste primarily comprises overburden and subgrade ore, which are systematically managed through designated waste dumps and stockpiles at operational sites. Stabilisation measures such as garland drains, toe walls and geo-coir matting are implemented to ensure environmental protection. Low-grade ore is preserved and utilised through blending and beneficiation initiatives, supporting resource conservation and reduction in waste generation.
Process-related waste, including tailings from beneficiation, is managed through tailing dams, with water recovery and reuse systems implemented to minimise discharge.
Hazardous wastes such as used oil, lubricants and contaminated materials are handled in accordance with the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016 and are disposed of through authorised recyclers.

Additional measures include sewage and effluent treatment plants, organic waste converters and biomedical waste management facilities at site hospitals, in compliance with applicable regulations.

3. With respect to the ecologically sensitive areas reported at Question 11 of Essential Indicators above, provide details of significant direct & indirect impact of the entity on biodiversity in such areas along-with prevention and remediation activities.
The Panna Diamond Mining Project of NMDC Limited is located in proximity to the Panna Tiger Reserve, within the Gangau Wildlife Sanctuary. Mining operations in such areas may have direct impacts, such as land disturbance and habitat modification and indirect impacts including dust generation, noise, surface runoff and changes in local hydrology.

Prevention measures, as specified in Environmental Management Plans (EMP), include controlled blasting techniques to minimise vibration and noise, regular monitoring of air, water and noise quality and development of greenbelt areas to reduce dust dispersion. Surface water management practices, such as garland drains and check dams, are implemented to control runoff and prevent sedimentation in nearby water bodies. Water management practices, including reuse and recycling, are adopted to minimise freshwater withdrawal and discharge.
Additional measures include water conservation initiatives such as development of storage reservoirs at project locations, including at the Panna project, which support both operational needs and surrounding ecosystems. Efforts to reduce environmental disturbance are also supported through optimised infrastructure usage, including reduced reliance on road-based transportation where feasible.
The project is subject to periodic environmental monitoring and compliance reporting to statutory authorities in line with EC conditions. Biodiversity management is further guided by the Company’s Biodiversity Policy, focusing on conservation, impact mitigation and responsible environmental management within operational areas.

NMDC operates six iron ore deposits in the Bailadila Sector of Chhattisgarh. To enhance iron ore evacuation, NMDC has taken up construction of slurry pipeline from Bailadila to Nagarnar at an estimated cost of INR 800 Crore. Currently, most iron ore production from Bailadila relies on the KK Railway line, which has limitations for transporting over 30 million metric tons per annum (MPTA). 3 Describe the mechanisms to receive and redress grievances of the community.
NMDC Limited addresses grievances of local communities through established stakeholder engagement practices at its operational locations.
At the project level, community concerns are addressed through interactions with site management and designated officials at mining locations. Community issues are typically received and addressed through ongoing engagement with local stakeholders, including village representatives and local authorities, as part of routine operational interface.
As a Central Public Sector Enterprise (CPSE), NMDC is part of the Government of India’s Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), which serves as a common grievance redressal platform for all CPSEs. Accordingly, grievances received through CPGRAMS are addressed by NMDC as part of its overall grievance redressal framework, in compliance with prescribed government timelines and procedures.

Grievances may also be submitted through formal communication channels, including written representations to project offices or the Company’s registered office, which are examined and addressed as per established administrative processes.
The Company’s approach to community grievance redressal is primarily based on project-level engagement and externally available government grievance platforms, ensuring that concerns raised by communities are received and addressed through established and compliant mechanisms.

2. Steps taken to inform and educate consumers about safe and responsible usage of products and/or services.
NMDC Limited operates predominantly in the B2B/B2G segment, supplying iron ore and related products to industrial users such as steel manufacturers. Accordingly, direct consumer-facing education on safe usage is not applicable. However, the Company supports safe and responsible usage of its products by providing detailed technical specifications, quality parameters and product characteristics through its website, contractual documentation and customer interactions. These inputs enable downstream industrial users to select appropriate material for their processes and operate within defined quality parameters, thereby supporting safe and efficient utilisation. As the products are used as industrial raw materials, responsibility for operational safety in usage lies with the downstream users and NMDC’s role is primarily limited to ensuring accurate product information and consistency in supply.

3. Mechanisms in place to inform consumers of any risk of disruption/discontinuation of essential services.
NMDC Limited operates primarily in the B2B/B2G segment as a supplier of iron ore and related bulk raw materials and does not provide essential services directly to end consumers. Accordingly, the requirement relating to disruption of essential consumer services is of limited applicability.
However, potential disruptions in supply are communicated to customers through established commercial arrangements and operational interfaces. These include provisions within contractual terms, direct communication with customers, notifications issued in connection with e‑auction processes and updates, where relevant, on the Company’s official website.
Through these mechanisms, NMDC supports timely communication of relevant information to its customers in line with its commercial practices.

Sustainability continues to be a defining element of NMDC’s growth journey. As a leading iron ore producer, we recognize that responsible mining requires us to create economic value while strengthening environmental stewardship, social development and sound governance. Guided by the principles of the United Nations Global Compact, NMDC is embedding sustainability considerations across its operations and decision-making processes.

Beyond climate and energy, NMDC continues to focus on responsible resource use and environmental protection. Process water is recycled and reused, with treatment through ETPs/STPs, for purposes such as horticulture wherever feasible. Our water stewardship is evident by the fact that we were able to achieve a 24% drop Year-on-Year in water intensity based on usable product. The Company continues systematic management of overburden, tailings, hazardous and non-hazardous wastes, together with progressive mine reclamation, plantation, ecological restoration and biodiversity-management measures.
During FY 2025–26, NMDC continued to advance its approach to sustainable and environment-friendly mining through focused action on energy efficiency, renewable energy, resource conservation, pollution control, water stewardship, biodiversity and responsible mine planning. Site-wise energy audits, digital monitoring of energy consumption, optimization of operating parameters, energy-efficient equipments, preventive maintenance and efficient mineral transportation are being pursued to improve operational efficiency.

NMDC’s sustainability journey is also centered on its host communities. The Company continued to support education, healthcare, technical education and sustainable employment opportunities in the tribal heartland. The Balika Shiksha Yojana continues to support the nursing education of students, while collaborations with leading medical and plastic-technology institutes have opened avenues for technical education and sustainable employment for students from Bastar, Chhattisgarh.
NMDC also continued to strengthen its renewable-energy footprint. The Company operates 10.5 MW of installed wind-energy capacity at Chitradurga, Karnataka, comprising seven 1.5 MW wind turbines, while solar installations across operating locations total 1.5 MW. During FY 2025–26, the wind assets generated approximately 21.5 million units of electricity, while solar energy consumption was approximately 1.33 million units.

NMDC recognizes that the transition to a lower-carbon mining sector requires continued innovation and collaboration. The Company is evaluating technologies including electrification and hybridization of mining equipment, in-pit crushing and conveying, advanced conveyor and gravity systems, digital mine optimization, energy-efficient comminution and beneficiation, lower-emission fuels and renewable-powered auxiliary systems. Adoption will be guided by technology readiness, mine-specific techno-economic feasibility, safety, reliability and measurable energy and emission benefits.
Energy efficiency remained an important component of NMDC’s decarbonization pathway. The measures undertaken across mining, beneficiation and material-handling operations have helped institutionalize energy monitoring and improve the efficiency of energy use. Energy consumed per tonne of usable product reduced by 10.2% in FY 2025–26 compared with FY 2024– 25, while energy consumption per unit of revenue declined by 18%.

While the progress made during FY 2025–26 is encouraging, NMDC remains conscious of the challenges and opportunities ahead. We will continue to deepen engagement with employees, suppliers, customers, local communities, policymakers and other stakeholders, and strengthen systems for measurement, monitoring and accountability. Our commitment is to build a responsible, resilient and future-ready mining enterprise that contributes meaningfully to people, the planet and India’s long- term development.
NMDC is progressing towards cleaner and more efficient mineral transportation. The slurry pipeline and doubling of the Kothavalasa–Kirandul railway line are near completion and are expected to reduce dependence on road transportation, fuel consumption and associated emissions. Downhill and gravity- assisted conveyors, efficient material-handling systems and other lower-energy transportation solutions are also being developed and evaluated.

The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the Standalone Financial Statements, whether due to fraud or error.

The Company’s Management is responsible for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls based on the internal controls with reference to financial statements criteria established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (‘ICAI’). These responsibilities include the design, implementation and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to the respective company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely preparation of reliable financial information, as required under the Act.

1.2.1 Basis of preparation
(a) Statement of compliance
NMDC Limited (the company) is a Navaratna Public Sector Enterprise under the Ministry of Steel, Government of India and single largest producer of iron ore in India. It owns and operates highly mechanized iron ore mines in the state of Chhattisgarh and Karnataka and has its registered office at Hyderabad, Telangana. It also operates the only mechanized diamond mine in India at Panna, Madhya Pradesh. NMDC has its own R&D Centre at Hyderabad which is recognized as a Centre of Excellence by UNIDO. During the FY 2025-26, the Company has commenced coal mining operations at Tokisud in the state of Jharkhand.
The standalone financial statements have been prepared in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards (“Ind AS”) notified under the Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, as amended and other relevant provisions of the Act.
(b) Basis of measurement
The standalone financial statements have been prepared on a historical cost convention and on an accrual basis, except for the following material items that have been measured at fair value as required by relevant Ind AS:

The standalone financial statements have been prepared on a historical cost convention and on an accrual basis, except for the following material items that have been measured at fair value as required by relevant Ind AS:
The Company is producing about over 53 MTPA of iron ore from its major iron ore producing units i.e. from Bailadila Sector in Chhattisgarh and Donimalai in Bellary-Hospet region in Karnataka. NMDC envisages to have an iron ore production capacity of 100 MNT by FY2030. The shares of the company are listed and traded on the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE), The Calcutta Stock Exchange Ltd and Bombay Stock Exchange India Limited (BSE).

x. Revenue recognition

x. Revenue recognition
A contract liability is the obligation to transfer goods or services to a customer for which the Company has received consideration (or an amount of consideration is due) from the customer. If a customer pays consideration before the Company transfers goods or services to the customer, a contract liability is recognised when the payment is made or the payment is due (whichever is earlier). Revenue from contracts with customers is recognized when control of the goods or services is transferred to the customer at an amount that reflects the consideration which is net off discounts and price concessions to which the Company expects to be entitled in exchange for those goods or services.
If the consideration in a contract includes a variable amount, the Company estimates the amount of consideration to which it will be entitled in exchange for transferring the goods to the customer. b) Deferred income tax

b) Deferred income tax
Deferred income tax is recognized using the balance sheet approach. Deferred income tax assets and liabilities are recognized for deductible and taxable temporary differences arising between the tax base of assets and liabilities and their carrying amount in financial statements, except when the deferred income tax arises from the initial recognition of goodwill or an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and affects neither accounting nor taxable profits or loss at the time of the transaction. Deferred income tax asset are recognized to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which the deductible temporary differences, and the carry forward of unused tax credits and unused tax losses can be utilized. Deferred income tax liabilities are recognized for all taxable temporary differences. The carrying amount of deferred income tax assets is reviewed at each reporting date and reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profit will be available to allow all or part of the deferred income tax asset to be utilized. Deferred income tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period when the asset is realized or the liability is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted at the reporting date.

Where the Company receives non-monetary grants, the asset is accounted for on the basis of its acquisition cost. In case a non-monetary asset is given free of cost it is recognised at a fair value. When loan or similar assistance are provided by government or related institutions, with an interest rate below the current applicable market rate, the effect of this favorable interest is recognized as government grant. 1.3 : Brief description of major contingent liabilities:
1.3.1 Tax on Mineral Rights and Mineral Bearing Land, Karnataka:

1.3.1 Tax on Mineral Rights and Mineral Bearing Land, Karnataka:
The Karnataka Legislature passed the Karnataka (Mineral Rights and Mineral Bearing Land) Tax Bill, 2024 in December 2024. As of the reporting date, the Bill is pending enactment, awaiting the assent of the Hon’ble President of India. Based on the legal opinion obtained by the Company, since, the Hon’ble Governor of Karnataka has referred the Bill for Presidential assent along with reservations on the legality of the said bill, it cannot be treated as law unless and until such assent is received.
The Bill, in its present form, proposes retrospective applicability of tax on mineral rights and mineral-bearing lands. Should it be enacted as currently drafted, the Company may be liable to pay tax amounting to approximately `15,481.72 crore (PY `13,975.07 crore), as on the reporting date. However, considering the pending legislative process, the reservations of the Governor, and the ongoing stakeholder discussions, this amount has been considered as contingent liability (refer 2.48.A 1.1a).

Further, as per the terms of the Long-Term Agreements and the Auction Notices, any future imposition of statutory duties, levies, or taxes is contractually recoverable from customers/bidders. Upon enactment of the Bill, the Company will assess the enforceability of such recourse provisions and take appropriate legal action to recover the applicable amounts from concerned parties.
1.3.2 Common Cause notice of the District Collector, Dantewada:
The Company received Show Cause Notices dated July 31, 2018, from the District Collector, South Bastar, Dantewada, demanding `7,241.35 crores as compensation, based on the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment in the Common Cause case (W.P. (C) No. 114 of 2014) related to iron ore mines in Odisha. NMDC has been contesting the applicability of this judgment to its operations in Chhattisgarh.

Revised Show Cause Notices were issued on September 26, 2019, reducing the demand to `1,623.44 crores. Subsequently, demand notices dated November 15, 2019, were issued, directing NMDC to deposit the amount (`1,131.97 crores for Bacheli and `491.47 crores for Kirandul) within 15 days. Considering that the mining leases of the Company in the State of Chhattisgarh were due for renewal from March 31, 2020, the Company deposited `600 crores under protest and filed a writ petition before the Hon’ble High Court of Bilaspur and a revision application before the Mines Tribunal, Ministry of Mines, Government of India, seeking to set aside the demand.
The High Court, on February 19, 2020, directed no coercive action till March 12, 2020, though hearings were delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Matter was last listed on September 24, 2025, however, based on the prayer of learned counsel of the parties, the matter was adjourned and will be listed in due course.
The Mines Tribunal heard the matter on various dates, including March 9, 2022; June 28, 2023; September 13, 2023; January 10, 2024 and June 21, 2024. NMDC obtained the State Government’s response on October 23, 2023, and filed its rejoinder on August 2, 2024. Matter was last listed on November 13, 2025, but hearing could not take place and adjourned. The matter is pending and will be listed in due course.

Pending final adjudication, the `600 crores paid under protest is disclosed under “Other Non-Current Assets,” and the `1,623.44 crores demand is considered as “Contingent Liabilities” (refer 2.48.A 1.1b).
1.3.3 Penalty against Dispatch of Mineral without Railway Transit Pass:
The Company has received a show-cause notice dated August 29, 2024 from the District Collector, South Bastar, Dantewada, alleging mineral dispatches for the period from 01.04.2024 to 25.08.2024 without timely Railway Transit Passes (RTP), resulting in a penalty of ` 1,620.50 crores (PY ` 1,620.50 crores). As the Company pays royalty in advance, there is no resultant loss to the exchequer.
Challenging this Notice, the Company has filed Writ Petition No. 4747/2024 in the Hon’ble High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur. The matter was last listed on February 27, 2025 and stands adjourned. Since the above matter is sub-judice, the penalty amount of ` 1,620.50 crores on iron ore dispatches for the period from 01.04.2024 to 25.08.2024 has been considered as “Contingent Liabilities” (refer 2.48.A 1.1c).

1.3.4 Forest Permit Fee at Bailadila Sector:

1.3.4 Forest Permit Fee at Bailadila Sector:
The State Government of Chhattisgarh, through a notification dated June 14, 2002, imposed a transit permit fee of ` 7 per ton. Based on this, demand notices dated November 23, 2012, amounting to ` 144.62 crore (` 79.52 crore for Bacheli and ` 65.10 crore for Kirandul) were issued by the Divisional Forest Officer, Dantewada, for dispatches made during the period from June 14, 2002 to October 31, 2012.
The Company has challenged the demand before the Hon’ble High Court of Chhattisgarh, contesting the retrospective levy and citing that transit passes were neither issued by the Forest Department nor demanded at the time of actual transit. The matter was last listed on April 23, 2026 and adjourned.
As per the Long-Term Agreements with customers, the transit fee is contractually recoverable from them. However, to ensure uninterrupted operations, the Company paid ` 144.62 crore under protest (` 48 crore in December 2022 and ` 96.62 crore in February 2023).
Based on legal opinion, the amount has been recognised as recoverable in the books. Since the matter is sub judice, the same is also disclosed as a contingent liability (refer 2.48.A 1.1d).
1.3.5 Disputed claims under ‘ Karnataka Forest Act:

1.3.5 Disputed claims under ‘ Karnataka Forest Act:
The Government of Karnataka introduced Forest Development Tax (FDT) at 12% on the sale value of iron ore, effective from August 27, 2008. Company challenged the levy before the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka, which passed an interim order directing payment of 50% of the FDT—25% in cash and 25% by way of Bank Guarantee.
Pursuant to this, the Department issued a demand for ` 121.84 crore (25% of 12%) and interest of ` 17.93 crore for delayed payment. Company complied by paying ` 139.77 crore in cash and providing a Bank Guarantee for an equivalent amount.
On December 3, 2015, the Hon’ble High Court of Karnataka quashed the FDT levy by Govt. of Karntaka, and directed the refund of the amounts collected. Company lodged refund claims accordingly. However, the Government of Karnataka filed a Special Leave Petition before the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India, which has admitted the case and stayed the refund. The matter was last listed on April 29, 2026 and adjourned.
The total liability stands at ` 523.23 crore (FDT of ` 487.38 crore and interest of ` 35.85 crore). Of this, NMDC has recovered ` 253.99 crore (` 150.28 crore in cash and ` 103.71 crore in Bank Guarantees) from customers. 2.49.1. A - GENERAL DESCRIPTION OF DEFINED/CONTRIBUTORY BENEFIT PLANS :
1. Pension Fund scheme Defined Contribution Plan
The company’s contribution to the defined contribution pension scheme is remitted to a separate trust based on a fixed percentage of the eligible employees’ salary. Company’s liability is limited to the extent of fixed contribution.
2.49.1 . B Defined Benefit Plan
2. Provident fund The company’s contribution to the provident fund is remitted to a separate trust based on a fixed percentage of the eligible employees’ salary. Further, the company makes good the shortfall, if any, between the return from investments of trust and the notified rate of interest on actuarial valuation basis.

3. Gratuity Eligible amount of Gratuity is paid to the employees on separation as per the Payment of Gratuity Trust as per Gratuity Act which is superceded by the Social Security Code 2020 (w.e.f 21.11.2025). The gratuity scheme is funded by the company and managed by NMDC Group gratuity Trust. The liability for the gratuity under the scheme is recognised on the basis of actuarial valuation.
4. Settlement Allowance Employees are paid eligible amount at the time of retirement for their settlement by the NMDC Employees Superannuation Benefit Fund Trust. The liability for the same is recognised on the basis of the actuarial valuation.
5. Post Retirement Medical Facilities Retired employees opting for the Post Retirement Medical Benefit Scheme on contribution of prescribed amount can avail medical benefits as per the Scheme. The liability under the scheme is recognised on the basis of the actuarial valuation and the liability is funded to and managed by NMDC Employees Superannuation Benefit Fund Trust.

Family Benefit Scheme Monthly payments to disabled separated employees/legal heirs of deceased employees on deposit of prescribed amount, till the notional date of superannuation and the liability is funded to NMDC Employees Superannuation Benefit Fund Trust. The liability under the scheme is recognised on the basis of the actuarial valuation

The liability under the scheme is recognised on the basis of the actuarial valuation. The liability is funded to and managed by NMDC Employees Superannuation Benefit Fund Trust

g) Risk exposure:
Through the defined benefit plans, the Company is exposed to a number of risk, the most significant of which are detailed below.
i) Investment Risk
Most of the plan asset investments are in government securities, other fixed income securities with high rating grades and mutual funds/ ETFs ( Exchange Traded Funds). The fair value of these assets is subject to volatility due to change in interest rates and other market & macro-economic factors. There is also a risk of asset liability matching i.e the cash flow for plan assets does not match with cash flow for plan liabilities.
ii) Change in discount rate:

ii) Change in discount rate:
The present value of defined benefit plan liabilities is calculated using a discount rate which is determined by reference to government bond’s’ yields at the end of the reporting period. A decrease (increase) in discount rate will increase ( decrease) present values of plan liabilities, although this will be partially offset by an increase in the value of the plans’ investments.
iii) Mortality rate risk
The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the best estimate of the mortality of plan participants both during and after their employment. As increase in the life expectancy of the plan participants will increase the plan’s liability.
iv) Salary escalation risk
The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the future salaries of plan participants. As such, an increase in the salary of the plan participants will increase the plan’s liability.
v) Turnover rate/Withdrawal rate of employee
If the actual employee withdrawal rate in the future turns out to be more or less than expected then it may result in increase/decrease in the liability.
vi) Medical inflation risk

vi) Medical inflation risk
The present value of the defined benefit plan liability is calculated by reference to the future medical expenditure of plan participants. As such, an increase in the medical expenditure of the plan participants will increase the plan’s liability.
G. Valuation of PF Trust Investments.
The analysis of the Fair Value of the NMDC EPF Trust investment has been carried out as on 31st March 2026 through a registered valuer. The fair valuation is carried out based on Market Approach and Income Approach. Market approach is followed for instruments such as Government Securities, frequently / infrequently traded listed corporate bonds, PSU bonds and Mutual Funds. Income Approach is followed for infrequently trade listed corporate bonds and other less liquid instruments, theoretical fair values calculated using the discounted cash flow method.

A. Basis for segmentation

A. Basis for segmentation
An operating segment is a component of the company that engages in business activities from which it may earn revenues and incur expenses and for which discrete financial information is available. All operating segments’ operating results are reviewed regularly by the Board of Directors to make decisions about resources to be allocated to the segments and assess their performance.
The company has three reportable segments, as described below, which are the company’s strategic business units. These business units offer different products and services, and are managed separately because they require different technology and marketing strategies. For each of the business units, the company’s Board reviews internal management reports on a periodic basis. Iron Ore being major segment contributes about 78.35% (PY 96.35%) of total revenue of the company, HR Coils contributes to 12.55% (PY 0.84%) and all other items consisting of Iron Ore Pellets, Wind Power sales contribute to 9.10% (PY 2.81%)of total revenue

iv) Advance to Karnataka Vijayanagar Steels Ltd (KVSL):
The Company has paid an advance of `639.61 crores to Karnataka Industrial Area Development Board (KIADB) towards the cost of 2,857.54 acres of land allotted to its wholly owned subsidiary, Karnataka Vijayanagar Steel Limited (KVSL), for setting up a 3 MTPA integrated steel plant. The land was allotted on a lease-cum-sale basis vide letter dated July 13, 2017. Possession certificates for 2,843.98 acres were issued on January 11, 2018, and revised on August 1, 2018. The land is currently in the possession of KVSL; however, the lease agreement is yet to be executed.
As per allotment conditions, construction was to commence within 9 months and production within 5 years from the date of possession. KVSL has requested an extension of the lease period to 99 years, which is currently under review by the Government of Karnataka. KIADB has, in principle, agreed to a 10-year lease in place of the earlier 2-year period.

To evaluate alternate business models, NMDC had appointed Business Management Consultant for KVSL. The said Consultant submitted their report to the Board of KVSL during December 2025. Management of the Company formed an internal committee to review the said report of the Consultant. Further, legal opinions are also obtained with respect to impact on surrender of Land. The recommendations of the said committee along with the legal opinions will be placed before the Board of Directors of KVSL for a final decision and thereafter appropriate action will be taken on this matter. If it is decided not to proceed with any project, Clause 9 of the Land Allotment Letter dated July 13, 2017, allows for voluntary surrender of the land, subject to a penalty of 15% on the amount paid

2.51.6: Impact Assessment of New Labour Codes
The Government of India has consolidated 29 existing labour legislations into a unified framework comprising four Labour Codes, namely: the Code on Wages, 2019; the Code on Social Security, 2020; the Industrial Relations Code, 2020; and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (collectively referred to as the New Labour Codes). These New Labour Codes have been made effective from November 21, 2025. The corresponding central rules under these codes were notified by the Central Government on May 8, 2026.

Based on actuarial valuation, the incremental impact of these changes, assessed by the Company, on the basis of the information available, consistent with the guidance provided by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, has been recognised in the financial statements of the Company for the year ended 31 March 2026, which is not material.

2.51.11: Un-Authorized removal of Iron Ore from Kumaraswamy Iron Ore Mine

2.51.11: Un-Authorized removal of Iron Ore from Kumaraswamy Iron Ore Mine
On 16 January 2026, a truck carrying 20 tonnes of iron ore from Kumaraswamy Iron Ore Mine (KIOM) was intercepted and seized by Sandur Police near Babai Cross due to the absence of valid transport document. FIR was lodged accordingly. Internal Departmental Enquiry Committee was constituted by the Company to enquire into the matter and to ascertain the facts and circumstance leading to the occurrence. On verification, another 6 vehicles were identified which exited the mines without proper documents for which complaint was lodged with the Police. Thus, the total un-authorized removal of Iron Ore from KIOM is 280 tons (7 vehicles).
Parallelly, NMDC Vigilance Department undertook an independent inquiry. Based on the Vigilance Dept. inquiry report, disciplinary proceedings were initiated. Detailed enquiry is under process and appropriate action will be taken by the Competent Authority accordingly. The total impact based on the cost of production and statutory levies for 280 tons of iron ore works out to ` 10.82 lakhs. Subsequent to the year end, a drone survey of iron ore through an external agency was carried out and the variation was found to be not material.

Further, as per the recommendations of the vigilance department, system improvement measures have been initiated to remediate the deficiencies/ strengthen the internal controls including enhancement of gate controls, surveillance systems, reconciliation processes and supervisory monitoring mechanisms which were in various stages of implementation as at March 31, 2026.

2.51.13 Compliance with Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 – Audit Trail Requirement
As per the proviso to Rule 3(1) of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014, effective from April 1, 2023, companies using accounting software are required to maintain an audit trail of every transaction, capturing an edit log of changes along with corresponding timestamps, and ensuring that such audit trails cannot be disabled.

The Company uses SAP S/4 HANA ERP for maintaining its books of account since FY 2020–21. Audit trail functionality has been enabled at the application level for key tables, in line with industry-standard practices. Administrative access to the database is restricted and secured through HANA Studio, and all admin-level activities are logged. However, the default audit logging at the database level is not currently enabled due to performance and storage considerations. The management remains committed to ensuring effective implementation of these statutory requirements.
During the year, on May 21, 2025 two additional application servers were deployed. The feature of recording audit trail (edit log) facility on these two servers was enabled on January 11, 2026 and has been operational thereafter. The audit trail (edit log) feature was not enabled for certain custom (Z) tables within the accounting software which was enabled subsequent to the year-end on April 23, 2026.
The audit trail has been preserved by the Company as per the statutory requirements for record retention.

Liquidity risk is the risk that the Company will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial liabilities that are settled by delivering cash or another financial asset. The Company’s approach to managing liquidity is to ensure, as far as possible, that it will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they are due, under both normal and stressed conditions, without incurring unacceptable losses or risking damage to the Company’s reputation.
Typically the Company ensures that it has sufficient cash on demand to meet expected operational expenses for a period of 60 days, including the servicing of financial obligations; this excludes the potential impact of extreme circumstances that cannot reasonably be predicted, such as natural disasters. In addition, the Company has taken fund based limits with banks to meet its short term financial obligations.

C. Market risk
Market risk is the risk that changes in market prices, such as foreign exchange rates and interest rates will affect the Company’s income or the value of its holdings of financial instruments. The objective of market risk management is to manage and control market risk exposures within acceptable parameters, while optimising the return.

(i) Foreign currency risk
Since majority of the company’s operations are being carried out in India and since all the material balances are denominated in its functional currency, the company does not carry any material exposure to currency fluctuation risk.
The Company’s exposure to foreign currencies is minimal and hence no sensitivity analysis is presented.
(ii) Interest rate risk
Interest rate risk is the risk that the fair value or future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market interest rates. The company quite often bridges its short term cash flow mismatch by availing unsecured working capital loans from banks or against its fixed deposits. Such loans have a very short tenure and the interest rate on such loans is based upon the fixed rates offered by banks on fixed deposits, increased by a few basis points or the rate of interest applicable for unsecured loans. Since the interest rates on fixed deposits are fixed, the company does not have any interest rate risk on such loans availed on a loan to loan basis.
The Company’s exposure to interest rate risk is minimal and hence no sensitivity analysis is presented.
